historical_timeline.summary: Born Freda Josephine McDonald in St. Louis, Missouri.
Comes to Paris with her troupe and performs at the Théâtre des Champs-Elysées.
Marries a Frenchman and becomes a French citizen.
Taken urgently to hospital in Casablanca after the loss of a pregnancy; in bed until December 1942, with five operations.
Adopts twelve children, raised at Les Milandes.
Receives the Legion of Honor and the Croix de guerre with palm for her Resistance work.
Speaks at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
Televised appeal for donations to save Les Milandes from its debts.
Evicted from Les Milandes; has a heart attack the same day and is admitted to hospital in Périgueux.
Heart attack and stroke after a concert in Copenhagen.
Dies in Paris of a cerebral hemorrhage, days after the opening of her fiftieth-anniversary revue at Bobino.

claims.statement: In North Africa during the war she was taken urgently to hospital in Casablanca, where she stayed in bed from June 1941 to December 1942, had five operations and was several times reported to be dying; she continued her intelligence work from her room.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for her long, grave illness; the dates and the number of operations come from La Croix, and Women in World History agrees that she was critically ill and had several operations.

claims.statement: The illness followed the loss of a pregnancy in 1941, given as a stillbirth in Casablanca by one source and as a miscarriage by another; the second account says a severe infection required a hysterectomy, after which she developed peritonitis and septicemia. La Croix says she was unable to have children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and partly conflicting account: stillbirth (Women in World History) or miscarriage (Women's History Network); the hysterectomy, peritonitis and septicemia rest on the Women's History Network alone. Whether her ovaries were removed is not recorded in any source read. Used, with this uncertainty, for the gynecologic history and the cardiovascular risk discussion.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Secondary prevention in the first months after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction in a 62-year-old Black woman, an entertainer, veteran and civil rights activist under heavy financial strain, seen three weeks after a stent with breathlessness on exertion. The episode covers the care women, and Black women in particular, are less likely to receive after a heart attack, as AHA statements and registry data show: a full cardiology review, echocardiography, cardiac rehabilitation and every guideline-directed medicine. It teaches dual antiplatelet therapy for twelve months, recognizing ticagrelor-related breathlessness and switching to clopidogrel with a loading dose rather than stopping; high-intensity atorvastatin with an LDL goal below 70 mg/dL and a single lipoprotein(a) measurement; a beta-blocker for the first year and an ACE inhibitor for high blood pressure, with potassium and kidney checks (one missed check recorded honestly); depression screening after a heart attack with the PHQ-2 and PHQ-9, as the AHA advises; a nosebleed on dual antiplatelet therapy managed without stopping it; a graded return to the stage after an exercise test; the hysterectomy of her thirties as a possible early menopause and a risk-enhancing factor; and trauma-informed, respectful care that takes her account of her body seriously, under the 2023 AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline, the 2025 ACC/AHA acute coronary syndromes guideline and the AHA statement on myocardial infarction in women.

referral.question: Breathlessness and tiredness three weeks after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery, in a 62-year-old woman. Please assess the cause of the breathlessness and her heart function, review her antiplatelet therapy and other medicines, and advise on cardiac rehabilitation and a return to performing on stage
referral.urgency: Soon; on the day of her two-week visit, after the echocardiogram that morning
referral.pertinent_history: Singer and dancer, decorated veteran and civil rights activist, under heavy financial strain after the recent loss of her home and estate; mother of twelve adopted children. Pressure in the chest that she first took for strain, with admission the next morning to a regional hospital: non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, 90% stenosis of the mid right coronary artery treated with one drug-eluting stent, mild disease elsewhere; LDL 146 mg/dL and high blood pressure found during the stay. Discharged on aspirin 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate 25 mg, lisinopril 5 mg and nitroglycerin as needed. Since discharge, breathlessness on one flight of stairs and tiredness, without chest pain. Today: blood pressure 138/84, pulse 64, oxygen saturation 98%; lungs clear; no edema. ECG: sinus rhythm, small inferior Q waves, no acute change. Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 264, creatinine 0.82 mg/dL (eGFR 81), potassium 4.4 mmol/L, LDL 84 mg/dL after three weeks of atorvastatin, hemoglobin A1c 5.6%. PHQ-9 7, with no thoughts of self-harm. Never smoker. A long illness in her thirties after the loss of a pregnancy, reportedly with an emergency hysterectomy; whether the ovaries were removed is not known. Enrolled in cardiac rehabilitation today. Lipoprotein(a) ordered. She asks to be listened to and to have each medicine explained

consultant_note.history: Ms. Baker, a 62-year-old singer and dancer, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashby-Nwosu five weeks after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery. She waited until the morning to go to hospital, thinking the pressure in her chest was the strain of losing her home. Since discharge she has had episodes of air hunger, a sudden need to take a deep breath, often while sitting or talking, beginning two or three days after leaving the hospital; they do not build with effort and come with no chest pressure, palpitations, orthopnea, cough or ankle swelling. Two cardiac rehabilitation sessions have not been limited by breath. She takes all her medicines and has not needed nitroglycerin. She has never smoked. She gave a clear account and asked to understand each choice
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Ashby-Nwosu's intake note and the hospital discharge summary: non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, 90% mid right coronary artery stenosis with one drug-eluting stent, mild disease elsewhere, LDL 146 mg/dL. ECG at intake: sinus rhythm, small Q waves in II, III and aVF, no acute change. Echocardiogram this morning: ejection fraction 52%, hypokinesis of the basal and mid inferior wall, normal right ventricle, normal estimated filling pressures, no thrombus, normal valves. Intake laboratory tests: hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 264, creatinine 0.82 mg/dL (eGFR 81), potassium 4.4 mmol/L, LDL 84 mg/dL, ALT 24 U/L, hemoglobin A1c 5.6%. Lipoprotein(a) 172 nmol/L. Home blood pressure average 136/82

exam.finding: Well; talking in full sentences; blood pressure 136/82, pulse 62; oxygen saturation 98% on room air
Regular rhythm; normal heart sounds; no murmur or gallop; right radial access site healed

assessment.assessment: Ticagrelor-related breathlessness, with some deconditioning. The pattern is typical: air hunger at rest beginning within days of the start, without effort-related chest symptoms, with a normal oxygen saturation, clear lungs, normal filling pressures and no anemia. It is not a sign of heart damage or of a blocked stent, but it is distressing and leads some patients to stop their medicine. There is no sign of heart failure or of ongoing ischemia

The ejection fraction of 52% with inferior hypokinesis matches the infarct in the right coronary territory; function is at the lower limit of normal. No further imaging or stress testing is needed now. Repeat the echocardiogram only if her symptoms change

Ticagrelor is preferred over clopidogrel after an acute coronary syndrome, but changing to clopidogrel is appropriate when ticagrelor causes breathlessness that affects adherence. Change with a 600 mg loading dose of clopidogrel 24 hours after the last ticagrelor dose, then 75 mg daily, without a gap. Her bleeding risk is not high, so dual antiplatelet therapy should continue for twelve months from the infarction, then aspirin 81 mg alone

Metoprolol succinate is appropriate for the first year after the infarction and, because she has high blood pressure, beyond it. Lisinopril is indicated for high blood pressure; raise it to 10 mg for a target below 130/80 mmHg, with potassium and creatinine one to two weeks later. LDL goal below 70 mg/dL with at least a 50% fall; her lipoprotein(a) of 172 nmol/L is an inherited risk-enhancing factor that statins do not lower, so reaching the LDL goal matters more, and ezetimibe should be added if LDL stays at 70 mg/dL or higher

She can begin light dance practice within the rehabilitation program now. Before full performances, which can demand 6 to 9 METs, a symptom-limited exercise test at about twelve weeks, on her usual medicines, will set her exercise prescription and show whether she can perform safely

A hysterectomy in her thirties, and a possible early menopause if ovarian function was lost, add to her risk and are recorded as risk-enhancing factors. Hormone therapy is not used to prevent heart disease. Women are less often given full secondary prevention and cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack, and more often have breathlessness, tiredness or other symptoms besides chest pain; her plan should be complete, and her account of her symptoms taken seriously. Screening for depression, which is common after a heart attack and worsens outcomes, is appropriate

recommendations: Stop ticagrelor; start clopidogrel 600 mg loading dose 24 hours after the last ticagrelor dose, then 75 mg daily

Continue aspirin 81 mg; dual antiplatelet therapy for twelve months from the infarction, then aspirin 81 mg alone; never interrupt it without speaking to cardiology, and manage minor bleeding without stopping it
Continue atorvastatin 80 mg; lipid panel four to eight weeks after the start; add ezetimibe if LDL is 70 mg/dL or higher
Continue metoprolol succinate 25 mg; raise lisinopril to 10 mg daily; potassium and creatinine in one to two weeks; target below 130/80 mmHg
Complete all 36 sessions of cardiac rehabilitation, with light dance practice there
Symptom-limited exercise test at about twelve weeks before a return to full performances
No repeat echocardiogram, stress imaging or angiography unless symptoms change
Repeat the PHQ-9 at about twelve weeks; use the rehabilitation program's psychologist
